opus-5.5.text:
I think disentangling superposition is a necessary step, but it's far from the whole picture. It's a bit like getting a dictionary for a language you don't speak. Suddenly you know the words, you can see "this direction corresponds to a concept like deception, or Python code, or the Golden Gate Bridge." That's a huge unlock, because before that you're staring at neurons that fire for a dozen unrelated things and you can't make heads or tails of it.

But knowing the vocabulary doesn't tell you the grammar. It doesn't tell you how those features combine, how information flows from one layer to the next, or what algorithm the model is actually running when it solves a math problem or decides to refuse a request. So the next frontier is really circuits: the interactions between features, the computational structure that sits on top of them.

And honestly, even at the feature level, I don't think we're close to complete. When you train sparse autoencoders, you find features at different granularities depending on how big your dictionary is. Some concepts split into finer and finer pieces as you scale up. So there's a real question about whether there's a "true" set of features at all, or whether we're imposing a convenient basis on something messier. There's also a lot of what people call dark matter, the reconstruction error, the part of the model's activity we're not explaining yet.

So if I had to put a rough number on it, I'd say we've mapped the coastline. We know there's a continent there and we can name some of the major landmarks, but the interior, how it all actually works together, is still largely uncharted. What's exciting is that the tools are getting good enough that we can start to do useful things, like steering models or debugging specific behaviors, even with an incomplete map. You don't need a perfect map to start navigating.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd be careful about the word "complete." Disentangling superposition is a huge step, because it means you've gone from looking at individual neurons that are doing five things at once to a set of features that each mean roughly one thing. That's the difference between having a dictionary and having a pile of letters. But a dictionary isn't an understanding of the language.

So I'd say superposition gets you the vocabulary. You've got features for, say, the Golden Gate Bridge, or a certain kind of sycophancy, or some syntactic pattern in code. What you don't automatically have is the grammar: how those features get composed, how they flow from one layer to the next, which ones are causally load-bearing for a given output versus just along for the ride. That's the circuit question, and it's much harder. You can have a very clean feature dictionary and still not be able to tell me why the model said what it said on a specific prompt.

There's also a coverage problem that people underestimate. When you train a sparse autoencoder or whatever your decomposition method is, you're always leaving some residual behind. You explain, call it, the bulk of the variance, and the rest is in this "dark matter" that your method didn't capture. And it's not obvious that the dark matter is unimportant. It might be exactly the rare, weird behaviors you most care about from a safety perspective, because those are the ones that don't show up often enough in the training distribution to earn their own feature.

And then there's the question of whether features at one scale are even the right level of description. You can split a feature into finer features and keep going, and at some point you're asking whether there's a natural grain to the model or whether we're imposing one. I genuinely don't know the answer to that yet.

So if you asked me to put a number on it, I wouldn't. I'd say we've gone from "we can't read this at all" to "we can read the nouns, and we're starting to be able to read some sentences." That's real progress. But the honest framing is that superposition was the first wall, and there are more walls behind it.

astra-6.text:
I think that would be a huge step, but I wouldn’t say the mapping is complete. Disentangling superposition might tell you what features the network represents. It doesn’t automatically tell you how the network uses those features to do a computation.

You’d still want to understand how features interact across layers, which pathways actually cause a particular output, and whether that explanation holds across different inputs. So you might have something like a vocabulary of the network’s internal representations, but you’d still need to figure out the grammar—how those representations get composed into behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think disentangling superposition would be a huge step, but I wouldn’t say you’ve completely mapped the network at that point. You might have a much better inventory of the features it represents, but you still need to understand how those features interact and how the computation unfolds across layers.

It’s the difference between knowing what the components are and knowing how the system works. If you identify a feature, can you predict when it activates? Can you intervene on it and reliably predict how the model’s behavior changes? And can you explain how it combines with other features to produce an answer? That’s where you start getting from a map of representations to an understanding of the computation.
